en: Excerpt from the *Shengwu ji*, Scroll Five: Tracing the Origins of the Tibetan Lamas.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shouyi of Wuzhong.
According to Tibetan sources, it is located outside Jiayuguan in Gansu. To the south of the east, there is Mount Qilian.
To the south of this mountain lies the Mongol Qinghai (Kokonor). To the southwest of Qinghai is the northeastern border of Tibet.
To the west of Ya’an in Sichuan, at Dajianlu in Songpan Prefecture, one travels several hundred li beyond the Great Wall and reaches Tibet.
Its eastern boundary serves as the primary postal station for the travel of government officials; this is the main thoroughfare of the official station.
It extends over six thousand li from east to west and more than three thousand li from south to north. It is situated approximately fourteen thousand li from the capital.
To the northwest it borders the Great Go-bi (Qarashahr), and to the southeast it reaches the Jinsha River in Yunnan. To the south...
To the west lies Burma; to the southwest lies the kingdom of Gorkha.
Since the Han and Tang dynasties, there has been the land of Uṣaḍiśa, which is present-day Tibet (Xīzàng); though the names differ, the place is the same.
Beyond the southwestern borders of Tibet lies the kingdom of Gorkha. To the west of Gorkha is the kingdom of East India. East India...
To the west of Duzhi lies Central India, which is the ancient land of the Buddhas.
The term *lǎmá* (喇嘛) is a respectful title for those from the Western Regions; translated into Chinese, it consists of the two characters "Wúshàng" (無上), meaning "Supreme.
It corresponds to the title "Héshàng" (和尚) used in China, which consists of the two characters "Lìshēng" (力生), meaning "Powerful Birth."
Since the time of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, Princess Wencheng was married to the King (Zanpu) of U-tsang as his consort;

she exclusively patronized Buddhism, constructing several hundred great stupas, temples, and monasteries. She invited Indian *bhadanta* (high-ranking monks) to Tibet to perform ritual recitations and provide spiritual instruction.
Throughout the Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties, there have likewise been high-ranking *bhadanta* [in Tibet]; thus, the Yuan...
The Shizu (Emperor Kublai) conferred upon Lama ’Phags-pa the title of Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) and Great Treasure Dharma King (Dabao Fawang).
His successors thereafter inherited this title and became the patriarchs of the Red Sect (the Sa-skya-pa).

Upon reaching the Yongle era of the Ming dynasty, the Emperor Chengzu conferred upon Latama Lama the title of Great Treasure Dharma King (Dabao Fawang) and Western Heaven Great Good Sovereign Buddha (Xitian Dashan Zizai Fo).
His three disciples were all appointed as National Preceptors (Guoshi).

Furthermore, he conferred the titles of Dharma King of the Mahāyāna (Dacheng Fawang), Dharma King of Great Virtue (Dade Fawang), and the five Dharma Kings of Propagation (Chanhua), Teaching (Chanjiao), Assistance (Fujiao), Protection (Hujiao), and Benevolence (Zanshan).

O King, furthermore, when the Dharma Kings—such as the "Son of the Buddha from the Western Heaven" (2), the "Great State Preceptor Consecrated by Empowerment" (9), and the "State Preceptor Consecrated by Empowerment" (18)—passed away, their disciples would unilaterally inherit their positions.

Gradually, these evolved into heterodox sects that vied for fame and seized territory. Furthermore, the successors of these various Dharma Kings first took wives and fathered sons, and only thereafter did they shave their heads to become monks.
As for the *lamas*, once the preceding *lama* has passed away, his son succeeds him by private inheritance and usurps his position.
He meets with his wife only on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month; on other days they do not meet. Although there are prohibitions against committing adultery, [they disregard them].

I do not know whether you will be able to observe these faithfully. As for the *lamas* who came from India to Tibet, they wore red robes upon their bodies; thus, they were called the "Red Tradition" (*dmar lugs*).
Later, as the Red Tradition flourished, it further divided into the "Flower Hat" and "Red Hat" sects, with a great many names and categories.
Regarding the Yellow Sect (Gelugpa): During the fifteenth year of the Yongle era, a man named Tsongkhapa was born in Xining Prefecture of Qinghai and became a *lamas*.
He first entered Tibet to join the Red Sect (Sakya/Kagyü), where he received scriptural instruction and practiced mantra recitation.

However, he observed that the followers of that sect were all cultivating supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), devoting themselves exclusively to such feats as swallowing swords and spitting fire to display wonders and delude the masses, rather than practicing the precepts.
This is the correct path of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Therefore, he departed and entered the Ganden Monastery within the Drepung complex.
At that monastery, he practiced meditation and attained the Way. He passed away in the fourteenth year of the Chenghua era.
When Tsongkhapa first began his spiritual training, he changed his attire and headgear to yellow, refusing to conform to those of the Red Hat school. Upon his death, Tsongkhapa left two testaments.
As for the great disciples: throughout successive lifetimes, they have manifested through reincarnation as *hubilhan* (reincarnate lamas), never losing sight of their original nature.
Being able to know their past lives, they return to serve as the presiding masters who hold the seat and govern the teachings. Of these two great disciples, one was named Dalai.
One was named Panchen, who by the Qianlong era had already undergone his sixth incarnation.
Furthermore, there was a great disciple of the First Dalai Lama named Chökyi Gyaltsen (Chabtsun Danba), whose lineage presided over the Mongolian Kumbum;
he too was able to emulate the Dalai and Panchen Lamas in ensuring that the *hübilhan* would not be mistaken.
Regarding his original nature and successive incarnations:
during the Kangxi era, there was another disciple of the Fifth Dalai Lama named Changja Hutuktu, who served as a State Preceptor (Guoshi) and Grand Lama (Dalama) during the Yongzheng period;
he was also able to ensure that the *hupirhan* [reincarnation] would not be mistaken for the original [incarnation].
He was reborn and resided permanently outside the capital of the Great Qing.
In the seventh year of the Chongde era of the Taizong of the Great Qing, he invited the Fourth Dalai Lama to Shengjing.
He was titled "Vajradhara Mahāsattva" and remained in the treasury. At the beginning of the Shunzhi era, an envoy was dispatched to welcome the Dalai Lama;

in the ninth year, he arrived at the capital, where he was conferred the title "Great Buddha of Universal Sovereignty of the Western Heaven," charged with overseeing the Buddhist teachings throughout the realm, and further invested as "Pung-u-je Ok-ji Da-lam-a."

The Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama presided over the two provinces of Tibet, the former and the latter, respectively. During the Qianlong era, the Lifanyuan (Court for Managing the Outer Regions) compiled a register;

by the time of the Sixth Dalai Lama, the number of monasteries under his jurisdiction totaled more than three thousand one hundred and fifty, with a total of approximately three hundred and twenty-five thousand lamas.
The Panchen Lama’s jurisdiction comprised three hundred monasteries.
There are twenty-seven locations with a total of thirteen thousand seven hundred and some monks.
The two Bolor tribes of the Red Sect also have one hundred and twenty temples and twenty-five thousand monks.
Including both the Red and Yellow sects, there are currently a total of three hundred and forty-one thousand one hundred and some monks.
How extraordinary! This may truly be called the pinnacle of prosperity.

As for other *lamas* who study the Way and are able to clarify the mind and realize their nature, they can only be designated as *Qutuqtu* upon receiving certification from the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama.
Only when one is able to remain undeluded regarding their original nature and returns in a successive incarnation can they be designated as a *Phurba* (Tulkus).

In total, regarding the capacities of the lamas who, through the transmigration of their consciousness into this world, emerged as *khubilgan* (reincarnations) and were entered into the registers of the Li Fan Yuan:
there were eighteen titled *tuktus* in Tibet; twelve titled *shab-lungs*;
nineteen in the Mongols of the North; fifty-seven in the Mongols of the South; and [a number] among the Tibetans of Qinghai.
There are thirty-five administrative districts (*sa*). Five are Tibetan territories in Chamdo, Sichuan; fourteen are *hutuktu* districts stationed in the capital.

In total, there are one hundred and sixty *hubilhan*. Only those who are able to obtain the title of *hutuktu* may exercise jurisdiction over the Tibetan subjects, acting like local chieftains (*tusi*).
The monastics outnumber the laity, and no secular officials are appointed; the ruler and the teacher are unified.

Situated between the monastic and lay communities, its ranks included the State Preceptor (Gushri), Chan Masters (Chanshi), Grand Lamas (Dalama), and the Zasag, who resided respectively among the various Tibetan districts and Mongol tribes;
all received their titles and emoluments from the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama.
As for military, judicial, and fiscal affairs, there were the Lamas serving as Desi (Regent), the Gablun (Cabinet Ministers), and the Taiji.
There were the *bong* [sword sheaths], the Khenpos, and the merchants who held superior offices and managed these affairs.
In the eighth year of the Jiaqing era, the Eighth Dalai Lama—the reincarnation of the Gushri Khan—manifested numerous spiritual signs.

Upon this being reported by the Ambans stationed in Tibet, he was requested to receive imperial edict for his enthronement and to preside over the teachings. To this day, several more incarnations have passed.
It is so.
